question: When oil becomes an imperial commodity, who supplies it, who is barred from it — and where do pressing and churning begin elsewhere?
summary: Under Rome, olive oil becomes a state-scale commodity. Monte Testaccio, a hill of some fifty million discarded oil jars, is its monument ([[ec1]]); the Tripolitanian olive boom turns Lepcis Magna's landowners into senators and then into the first African emperor ([[ec2]]); Caesar fines Leptis three million pounds of oil, and Lepcis later gives Rome an oil gift that creates a procurator for the oil annona ([[o2]], [[o3]]); and the beam, lever and screw presses are the machines ([[te1]]). Mattingly's rule of thumb of 20 litres a head implies a Mediterranean demand in the hundreds of millions of litres a year ([[ec3]]).

Elsewhere other fats take their own paths. In India ghee and sesame oil are exported and prescribed by season, and the Arthaśāstra gives cooking proportions of oil for the meat shop ([[x3]], [[th3]], [[ec5]], [[b1]]). In China the pressing of seeds for oil begins only in the late Han, an oil trade appears by about 290, and by 544 colza mills sell oil while lard and tallow still lead in the kitchen; the same manual teaches churning su, China's butter ([[te2]], [[ec4]], [[th4]], [[te4]]). In Egypt the Ptolemies tax five oils ([[o1]]).

The north keeps animal fat and butter. Rome's writers treat butter as the barbarian's fat, fit for poultices or hair, and the Germanic peoples who overrun the western empire bring, in Mueller's phrase, the ‘revenge of animal fat on imperial oil’ ([[e1]], [[th1]], [[th2]], [[w1]]).

Beyond the imperial frame the folio adds four smaller lights. Carthage’s farming manual, lost in Punic, reaches us only because Rome had it translated ([[th5]]); the sanctuary of Delos pays rents that follow the price of oil ([[ec6]]); Hanukkah makes a day’s lamp oil last eight ([[b2]]); and the domesticated coconut travels across the Pacific with the Polynesians, a fat tradition with no Roman or Indian text at all ([[ec7]]). In Egypt the Greek papyri of the Fayum name castor, radish, safflower, linseed, sesame and olive oils ([[ec8]]).

themes.title: Rome's oil economy
text: Jars, estates, taxes and presses: the best-quantified oil trade of antiquity, though the numbers are modern estimates.

themes.title: Butter and the barbarian
text: Roman medicine uses butter as a drug while Roman poets mock it as the northerners' hair-dressing; after 400, the northern fat culture advances.

themes.title: India: ghee, oil and medicine
text: The Vinaya's five medicines, Caraka's seasonal rule for ghee, the Arthaśāstra shop, and the Periplus's exports show fats as medicine, trade and cooking at once.

themes.title: China begins to press, and to churn
text: Needham reads the absence of pressed oil before the Han as an argument from silence; by 544 the Chhi min yao shu describes colza mills, perilla and sesame oils and a recipe for su.

themes.title: Other lights: Carthage, Delos, Jerusalem and the Pacific
text: Four entries that do not fit the imperial story: a lost Punic manual, an island sanctuary’s accounts, a lamp-oil legend and a coconut voyage whose date is only a placeholder.

turning_points.text: Ptolemy II taxes five oils in Egypt.
Caesar fines Leptis three million pounds of oil.
China learns to press oil from seeds.
Monte Testaccio rises in Rome; Tripolitania booms.
The Germanic peoples bring animal fat to the western empire.
The Chhi min yao shu records colza oil mills and the churning of su.

how_to_read: The Roman entries sit in *Economy*, *Order* and *Technology*; the Indian and Chinese ones in *Thought*. Read the Nexus for the Tripolitanian chain from estates to jars to Rome.
Note the numbers: they are Mattingly's and Foxhall's estimates, not Roman records, and their tier labels say so.

The *picture by region* counts the 27 entries: Europe 9, Near East 3, Far East 9, Africa 5, Oceania 1; none in Americas or Worldwide. Africa here is the Roman oil province seen from Rome, not the home of African fats.

sources.intro: A scholarly archaeology of Roman oil in Mattingly, a scholarly translation of Chinese farm and oil texts in Needham, popular histories for butter, and Achaya for India.
main: Mattingly, *Tripolitania* and ‘The Olive Boom’, for the Libyan estates, amphorae and annona ([[ec1]], [[ec2]], [[o2]], [[o3]], [[x1]], [[ec3]]).
Needham, SCC 6.5, for the Chinese presses, oils and su ([[te1]], [[te2]], [[ec4]], [[th4]], [[te4]]).
Achaya for India ([[th3]], [[ec5]], [[x3]]); Khosrova and Mueller for Rome's butter and the Germanic shift ([[th1]], [[th2]], [[e1]], [[w1]]); Dalby for Egypt ([[o1]]).
Foxhall for Delos ([[ec6]]); Mueller for Hanukkah ([[b2]]); encyclopedia and lecture notes found by search for Mago ([[th5]]); Kiple for the coconut ([[ec7]]).
Lucas, read from a scanned copy, for Egypt’s oils in the Greek papyri ([[ec8]]).
contested: Whether Caesar's fine was annual and which Leptis it fell on ([[o2]]); the Arthaśāstra's date ([[ec5]]).
The first pressing of oil in China is an argument from absence ([[te2]]).
The Germanic ‘revenge of animal fat’ is Mueller's interpretation ([[w1]]).
Dating of the Monte Testaccio dump is the folio's, not a cited figure ([[ec1]]).
Mago’s date is unsettled ([[th5]]); Mueller dates the Hanukkah miracle to 168 BC, where 164 BC is the usual year ([[b2]]); the coconut entry’s date is a placeholder ([[ec7]]).
gaps: Roman literary sources (Cato, Columella, Pliny) were not read directly; nor the Egyptian papyri.
Soap in antiquity rests on two passing mentions ([[te3]]).
Sub-Saharan Africa has no entry in this folio; the shea sequence at Kirikongo starts about 100 AD and is filed in the next folio ([[ec7]] in fats-600-1000).

text: Rome as consumer and administrator: the jars of Monte Testaccio, the per-head figure, the beam and screw presses, soap as a cosmetic, Gaul’s butter, Galen and Anthimus on butter, Delos’s rents and the Germanic shift ([[ec1]], [[ec3]], [[te1]], [[te3]], [[e1]], [[th1]], [[th2]], [[ec6]], [[w1]]).

Three entries: Ptolemy II’s tax on five oils in Egypt, the oils named in the Greek papyri of the Fayum, and the Hanukkah lamp-oil legend ([[o1]], [[ec8]], [[b2]]). Egypt is filed here by the atlas taxonomy, though the Tripolitanian and Punic oils are North African.

India and China each begin their own fat story: the Buddha’s five medicines, Caraka on ghee, the Arthaśāstra shop, the Periplus’s exports; China learns to press seeds and churn su, and sesame arrives by the Silk Road ([[b1]], [[th3]], [[ec5]], [[x3]], [[te2]], [[te4]], [[th4]], [[ec4]], [[x2]]).

Carthage and Tripolitania: Mago’s manual, Caesar’s fine on Leptis, the oil gift to Rome, the olive boom and Tripolitanian oil in Rome ([[th5]], [[o2]], [[o3]], [[ec2]], [[x1]]). All five entries are the Roman province seen from Rome. Sub-Saharan Africa has no entry; the shea record begins in the next folio.
No entry. Nothing in the library bears on American fats in these centuries.
One entry: the domesticated coconut carried by Polynesians, whose ancestral culture emerged in Tonga and Samoa in the second half of the first millennium BC ([[ec7]]).
